ROUNDUP_decimal_places.description: Rounds up to 2 decimal places even though the 3rd decimal (1) would round down normally

ROW_no_arg_uses_formula_cell.description: No argument: ROW() returns the row of the cell containing the formula itself. This case's formula lands in cell F1 by default, which is row 1
ROW_no_arg_uses_formula_cell.notes: The harness writes each case's formula into cell F1 (row 1, column 6); ROW() with no anchor argument returns the formula's own row, i.e. 1

ROW_explicit_cell_ref.description: Explicit single-cell reference argument overrides the formula's own location

ROW_range_returns_first_row.description: In non-array (scalar) context, ROW() of a multi-row range returns the row number of the FIRST row of the reference

ROW_far_cell.description: Sanity check with a larger row number

ROWS_basic_column_range.description: Height (row count) of a single-column range; does not depend on cell contents

ROWS_single_cell.description: A single cell reference has exactly 1 row

ROWS_2d_range.description: Row count of a 2-D range only counts rows, ignoring the 3 columns

RSQ_perfect_fit.description: A perfectly linear relationship has an R-squared of 1 (all variance explained)

RSQ_no_fit.description: Data with no linear relationship has an R-squared of 0. RSQ equals CORREL squared.

SEARCH_case_insensitive_match.description: SEARCH is case-insensitive: lowercase 'a' matches the leading uppercase 'A' -> position 1 (contrast with FIND on this exact same input, which is case-sensitive and returns #VALUE!)

SEARCH_wildcard_asterisk.description: SEARCH supports wildcards unlike FIND: '*' matches any sequence of characters, so "p*e" matches the substring "pple" starting at position 2
SEARCH_wildcard_asterisk.notes: Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/search-function-9ab04538-0e55-4719-a72e-b6f54513b495 - SEARCH allows the wildcard characters '?' and '*' in find_text; FIND does not support wildcards at all

SEARCH_wildcard_question_mark.description: '?' wildcard matches exactly one character, so "?pple" matches "Apple" starting at position 1

SEARCH_not_found.description: find_text not present anywhere in within_text -> #VALUE!

SECOND_of_fractional_day_noon.description: SECOND applied to a bare fractional-day serial -- exactly noon has 0 seconds past the minute

SECOND_of_time_value.description: SECOND applied to a TIME()-constructed value

SECOND_of_time_near_midnight.description: SECOND just before a day boundary

SEQUENCE_basic_vertical.description: Default rows-only sequence starting at 1, step 1

SEQUENCE_rows_cols.description: 2 rows x 3 columns filled row-major from 1

SHEET_returns_positive_index.description: SHEET() returns the current sheet's 1-based index; the absolute number depends on workbook structure (our harness batches many test sheets into one workbook), so we assert the invariant instead

SHEETS_returns_positive_count.description: SHEETS() counts sheets in the workbook; the harness workbook holds one sheet per test case, so we assert the invariant rather than a fixed count

SIGN_zero.description: Zero returns 0, not an error -- SIGN never errors on a numeric input

SIGN_small_negative_fraction.description: Any negative value, no matter how small, still returns -1

SLOPE_exact_line.description: Points on y=2x+1 exactly: least-squares slope must be exactly 2

SMALL_k1_equals_min.description: k=1 returns the same value as MIN

SMALL_k_out_of_range.description: k larger than the count of values -> #NUM!
SMALL_k_out_of_range.notes: Only 5 values exist; requesting the 6th-smallest is out of range

SMALL_k_zero_error.description: k=0 is also out of the valid 1..n range -> #NUM!

SORT_descending.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 5, got 1

SORT_by_second_column.description: 2D range sorted by its second column ascending

SORT_empty_range_error.description: Sorting a single blank cell (degenerate case)
SORT_empty_range_error.notes: Blank cell sorts as 0 in numeric context; no error expected; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 0, got None

SORTBY_by_other_col.description: Sort column A by the values in column B (ascending)
SORTBY_by_other_col.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 'y', got '#NAME?'

SQRT_zero.description: Square root of zero is zero

SQRT_negative_returns_num_error.description: Negative input has no real square root -> #NUM!
SQRT_negative_returns_num_error.notes: Microsoft's SQRT docs state verbatim: 'If number is negative, SQRT returns the #NUM! error value' -- https://support.microsoft.com/en-US/Excel/functions/sqrt-function

SQRT_documented_abs_workaround.description: Microsoft's own SQRT documentation demonstrates wrapping a possibly-negative argument in ABS as the standard workaround to avoid #NUM!
SQRT_documented_abs_workaround.notes: Same doc page above shows an example using '=SQRT(ABS(A2))' specifically to sidestep the negative-input #NUM! case

STANDARDIZE_above_mean.description: Converts a value to a z-score: 50 is two standard deviations above a mean of 40

STANDARDIZE_at_mean.description: A value equal to the mean has a z-score of 0

STANDARDIZE_below_mean.description: A value below the mean gives a negative z-score

STDEV_basic_two_points.description: Sample standard deviation of two hand-verifiable values

STDEV_matches_STDEV_S_same_data.description: Legacy STDEV on the classic Wikipedia sample dataset {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9}; compare to STDEV.S_matches_STDEV_same_data on identical data in the STDEV.S file - both must return exactly the same value since STDEV.S is just the modern name for the same sample-stdev calculation

STDEV_single_value_div0.description: Sample stdev needs at least 2 data points (divides by n-1); a single value -> #DIV/0!
STDEV_single_value_div0.notes: n-1=0 with a single supplied value, causing division by zero

STDEV.P_diverges_from_sample_same_data.description: Population standard deviation on the SAME dataset {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9} used for STDEV/STDEV.S - divides by n instead of n-1, giving a smaller, exact result (2) vs the sample stdev's 2.138089935299395

STDEV.P_two_points_diverges.description: Same two-point data as the sample-stdev cases (10,20) but population formula divides by n=2 instead of n-1=1, giving a much smaller result
STDEV.P_two_points_diverges.notes: Population variance=((10-15)^2+(20-15)^2)/2=25; sqrt(25)=5, vs sample stdev's 7.0710678118654755 on identical data

STDEV.P_single_value_no_error.description: Unlike STDEV.S/STDEV, a single value does NOT error for the population formula, since it divides by n (=1), not n-1
STDEV.P_single_value_no_error.notes: Population variance of one point = 0/1 = 0, a valid result - genuine divergence from STDEV.S's #DIV/0! on the same single-cell input

STDEV.S_basic_two_points.description: Sample standard deviation of two hand-verifiable values, identical formula/data to STDEV_basic_two_points in the STDEV file

STDEV.S_matches_STDEV_same_data.description: STDEV.S on the classic Wikipedia sample dataset {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9} - must match STDEV_matches_STDEV_S_same_data exactly, since STDEV.S is simply the Excel-2010+ modern name for the legacy STDEV calculation (same n-1 sample formula)

STDEV.S_single_value_div0.description: Sample stdev needs n>=2 (divides by n-1); one value -> #DIV/0!, confirmed against Microsoft's STDEV.S documentation of the n-1 method (https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/stdev-s-function-7d69cf97-0c1f-4acf-be27-f3e83904cc23)

STDEVA_numbers_only.description: For pure numbers STDEVA equals STDEV (sample standard deviation)

STDEVA_counts_text_as_zero.description: Unlike STDEV, STDEVA counts text as 0, so {2,4,"x"} is treated as {2,4,0}: sample standard deviation 2

STDEVA_identical_values.description: Identical values have zero standard deviation

STDEVP_textbook.description: Population standard deviation of the classic 8-value example (mean 5, variance 4)

STDEVP_two_values.description: Two values equidistant from their mean of 3 give a population standard deviation of 1

STDEVP_ignores_text.description: Text and blank cells are ignored, not treated as zero

STDEVPA_textbook.description: For pure numbers STDEVPA equals STDEVP (population standard deviation): the classic example gives 2

STDEVPA_counts_text_as_zero.description: Unlike STDEVP, STDEVPA counts text as 0, so {5,5,5,5,"x"} is treated as {5,5,5,5,0}: population standard deviation 2

SUBSTITUTE_all_occurrences.description: Without instance_num, every occurrence of old_text is replaced

SUBSTITUTE_instance_num.description: instance_num=2 replaces only the 2nd occurrence of old_text, leaving the 1st untouched

SUBSTITUTE_no_match.description: old_text not present in text returns the text unchanged

SUBSTITUTE_case_sensitive.description: SUBSTITUTE matches old_text case-sensitively; lowercase 'a' does not match the uppercase 'A' in "Apple", so the text is returned unchanged

SUBTOTAL_sum_code9.description: Function code 9 = SUM over visible rows (none hidden here)

SUBTOTAL_ignores_nested_subtotal.description: A5 contains its own SUBTOTAL over A1:A4; the outer SUBTOTAL must skip it (no double-count), so the answer is 100, not 200

SUM_basic_range.description: Basic sum of a contiguous numeric range

SUM_text_in_cell_reference_ignored.description: A text value stored in a referenced cell is IGNORED by SUM, not coerced to a number, even though it looks numeric
SUM_text_in_cell_reference_ignored.notes: A2 holds the text string '2' (not the number 2); SUM over a range skips text cells entirely, so the total is 1+3=4, not 6

SUM_literal_numeric_string_argument_coer.description: A numeric-looking TEXT LITERAL passed directly as a function argument (not via a cell reference) IS coerced to a number, unlike the same text sitting in a referenced cell
SUM_literal_numeric_string_argument_coer.notes: Contrast with SUM_text_in_cell_reference_ignored: Excel coerces literal string arguments that look like numbers when they are typed directly into the formula, but does not do so for text found inside a range reference

SUM_empty_range.description: Summing an entirely empty range returns 0, not an error

SUMIF_basic.description: Sum of cells in the range itself that satisfy the criteria (no sum_range)

SUMIF_separate_sum_range.description: Criteria evaluated against A but the matching B cells are summed
SUMIF_separate_sum_range.notes: Rows 3,4,5 satisfy A>2; sum of paired B = 30+40+50

SUMIF_wildcard_text.description: Wildcard text criteria matches cells starting with 'a'

SUMIF_blank_cells_ignored.description: Blank cells interspersed in the range are simply skipped, not treated as matching or as errors
SUMIF_blank_cells_ignored.notes: A2 and A4 are blank (unset); only A1,A3,A5 exist and all satisfy >0

SUMIFS_basic.description: Sum of A where paired B > 2

SUMIFS_wildcard.description: Wildcard text criteria matches 2 of 3 rows

SUMPRODUCT_basic.description: Sum of pairwise products across two equal-sized arrays

SUMPRODUCT_single_array_acts_like_sum.description: With only one array argument, SUMPRODUCT just sums its elements

SUMPRODUCT_boolean_double_negative_count.description: Classic double-unary-minus idiom coerces a boolean array to 1/0 to count matches without an extra helper column
SUMPRODUCT_boolean_double_negative_count.notes: A3,A4,A5 satisfy >2; --(...) turns TRUE/FALSE into 1/0 and SUMPRODUCT sums them

SUMPRODUCT_condition_times_values_sumif_.description: Multiplying a boolean condition array by a value array replicates SUMIF without a separate criteria function
SUMPRODUCT_condition_times_values_sumif_.notes: Rows where A>2 (rows 3,4,5) contribute their B value: 30+40+50=120

SUMPRODUCT_mismatched_array_sizes_error.description: Arrays of different dimensions cannot be multiplied element-wise -> #VALUE!
SUMPRODUCT_mismatched_array_sizes_error.notes: Microsoft docs: array arguments must have the same dimensions, otherwise SUMPRODUCT returns #VALUE!

SWITCH_default_value.description: Trailing unpaired argument acts as the default

TAKE_first_2x2.description: Take the first 2 rows and first 2 columns of a 3x3 range
TAKE_first_2x2.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 1, got '#NAME?'

TEXT_currency_format.description: Currency-style format code with thousands separator and 2 decimal places, rounding the value. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/text-function-20d5ac4d-7b94-49fd-bb38-93d29371225c (worked example)

TEXT_percentage_format.description: Percentage format code multiplies by 100, appends %, and rounds to 1 decimal place. Source: Microsoft TEXT docs worked example.

TEXT_scientific_format.description: Scientific-notation format code. Source: Microsoft TEXT docs worked example.

TEXT_zero_padding.description: Zero-padding format code pads with leading zeros to fill every '0' placeholder. Source: Microsoft TEXT docs worked example.

TEXT_iso_date_format.description: ISO-style date format code applied to a fixed, deterministic date (not TODAY()) so the result is reproducible.

TEXT_weekday_name_format.description: Full weekday name format code. March 5, 2024 falls on a Tuesday (verified against a real calendar).

TEXTAFTER_basic.description: Text after the first delimiter occurrence

TEXTAFTER_negative_instance.description: Negative instance_num counts delimiters from the end
TEXTAFTER_negative_instance.notes: -1 means the last delimiter; text after it is 'c'; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'c', got '#NAME?'

TEXTAFTER_not_found_custom.description: Delimiter not present with if_not_found supplied

TEXTBEFORE_basic.description: Text before the first delimiter occurrence

TEXTBEFORE_not_found_default.description: Delimiter not present and no if_not_found -> #N/A

TEXTBEFORE_not_found_custom.description: Delimiter not present with if_not_found supplied

TEXTBEFORE_negative_instance.description: Negative instance_num counts delimiters from the end
TEXTBEFORE_negative_instance.notes: -1 means the last delimiter; text before it is 'a-b'; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'a-b', got '#NAME?'

TEXTJOIN_ignore_empty_false.description: ignore_empty=FALSE keeps the empty string as a segment

TEXTJOIN_range.description: Joining a cell range with a delimiter

TEXTJOIN_multiple_ranges.description: Multiple ranges are flattened and joined in order

TEXTSPLIT_basic.description: Basic column split on a single delimiter
TEXTSPLIT_basic.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 'a', got '#NAME?'

TEXTSPLIT_row_and_col_delims.description: col_delimiter="," and row_delimiter=";" produce a 2x2 grid
TEXTSPLIT_row_and_col_delims.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 'a', got '#NAME?'

TEXTSPLIT_ignore_empty.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 'a', got '#NAME?'

TEXTSPLIT_pad_with.description: Uneven row lengths are padded with pad_with instead of #N/A
TEXTSPLIT_pad_with.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 'a', got '#NAME?'

TIME_basic.description: Ordinary in-range h/m/s construction returns the fraction-of-a-day serial

TIME_hour_wraps_modulo_24.description: Documented behavior: an hour argument greater than 23 wraps modulo 24 instead of erroring or accumulating past a single day. Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/time-function-9a5aff99-8f7d-4611-845e-747d0b8d5457 ("Any value greater than 23 will be divided by 24 and the remainder will be treated as the hour value")

TIME_doc_example_27_hours.description: The exact example given in Microsoft's own TIME documentation ("TIME(27,0,0) = TIME(3,0,0) = .125 or 3:00 AM")
TIME_doc_example_27_hours.notes: 27 mod 24 = 3 -> TIME(3,0,0) = 3/24 = 0.125, matching the cited doc example verbatim

TIMEVALUE_6am.description: 6 AM is a quarter of the way through the day

TOCOL_flatten_by_row.description: Flatten a 2x2 range into a single column, scanning by row

TODAY_exists_and_plausible.description: Existence probe only: TODAY() is non-deterministic (changes daily), so there is no fixed 'expected' value
TODAY_exists_and_plausible.notes: Non-deterministic by design; harness/human should only check the engine recognizes the function (not #NAME?/#VALUE!) and returns a plausible large positive integer serial

TODAY_year_is_plausible.description: Wrapping TODAY() in YEAR() gives a coarser but still non-deterministic probe
TODAY_year_is_plausible.notes: Non-deterministic; harness/human should only check the result is a plausible 4-digit year (>= 2026 as of this test's authoring)

TODAY_self_difference_is_deterministic.description: Even though TODAY() itself is volatile, two calls within the SAME recalculation pass must return the identical value, so their difference is always exactly 0 -- a genuinely deterministic assertion about a volatile function
TODAY_self_difference_is_deterministic.notes: Both TODAY() calls are evaluated as part of one recalculation of one cell, so they cannot differ

TOROW_flatten_by_row.description: Flatten a 2x2 range into a single row, scanning by row

TRANSPOSE_row_to_column.description: 1x3 horizontal row transposed into a 3x1 vertical column

TRANSPOSE_2x3_to_3x2.description: 2 rows x 3 columns transposed into 3 rows x 2 columns

TRANSPOSE_single_cell_degenerate.description: Degenerate 1x1 case: transposing a single cell yields the same single value

TRANSPOSE_blank_cell_becomes_zero.description: A blank source cell transposes to 0, not an empty string, matching normal blank-cell-in-formula behavior
TRANSPOSE_blank_cell_becomes_zero.notes: B1 is left unset (blank); its transposed position reads back as 0; MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 0, got None

TREND_extrapolate_exact_line.description: y=2x data extrapolated to x=5 must give exactly 10

TRIM_collapse_and_strip.description: Leading/trailing spaces are stripped and multiple interior spaces collapse to a single space

TRIM_tab_not_removed.description: TRIM only removes the regular ASCII space character (decimal 32); it does NOT remove other whitespace such as a tab (CHAR(9)), so the leading tab survives untouched
TRIM_tab_not_removed.notes: Microsoft docs: "the TRIM function was designed to trim the 7-bit ASCII space character (value 32) from text" -- it does not generalize to other whitespace. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/trim-function-410388fa-c5df-49c6-b16c-9e5630b479f9; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '\tHello', got 'Hello'

TRIM_nonbreaking_space_not_removed.description: TRIM does not remove the non-breaking space character (CHAR(160), HTML  ) even though it renders as whitespace -- a real, documented, and easy-to-miss cross-engine divergence point since data pasted from web pages is full of CHAR(160)
TRIM_nonbreaking_space_not_removed.notes: Microsoft docs state explicitly: "by itself, the TRIM function does not remove the nonbreaking space character (which has a decimal value of 160 and is commonly used in web pages as the HTML entity  )." Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/trim-function-410388fa-c5df-49c6-b16c-9e5630b479f9

TRIM_single_spaces_untouched.description: A string with only single spaces between words passes through unchanged

TRIMMEAN_drop_extremes.description: Trim 40% (one from each end), average the rest

TRUE_zero_arg_function.description: The zero-argument function form TRUE() is callable and returns the logical value TRUE, per https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/true-function-7652c6e3-8987-48d0-97cd-ef223246b3fb

TRUE_equals_keyword.description: TRUE() returns a genuine logical value equal to the bare TRUE keyword

TRUE_in_if.description: TRUE() used as a condition behaves exactly like the TRUE keyword

TRUNC_basic_positive.description: Positive fractional number truncates its decimal part (same result as INT here)

TRUNC_negative_truncates_toward_zero.description: Documented classic divergence from INT: TRUNC simply removes the fractional part with no rounding, i.e. truncates TOWARD zero
TRUNC_negative_truncates_toward_zero.notes: Per Microsoft's TRUNC function docs, TRUNC(-8.9) = -8 (fractional part discarded, toward zero), whereas INT(-8.9) = -9 (rounds down, away from zero) -- see the paired INT_negative_rounds_toward_negative_infinity case in INT.json

TRUNC_num_digits_positive.description: num_digits=2 keeps two decimal places, discarding the rest without rounding
TRUNC_num_digits_positive.notes: 3.14159 truncated (not rounded) at 2 decimals is 3.14; if it were ROUND instead, 3.14159 would still round to 3.14 here, but TRUNC(3.145,2) vs ROUND(3.145,2) would diverge -- this case isolates the num_digits mechanic, not the rounding-vs-truncating distinction

TRUNC_negative_num_digits.description: Negative num_digits truncates digits to the LEFT of the decimal point
TRUNC_negative_num_digits.notes: Negative num_digits zeroes out the last 2 digits of the integer part without any rounding

TYPE_error.description: An error value -> code 16. TYPE classifies the error's TYPE rather than propagating the error itself, matching ISERROR-style special-casing

UNICHAR_accented_char.description: Basic code point beyond the 7-bit ASCII/basic-Latin range (U+00E9 'e with acute')

UNICHAR_roundtrip_via_unicode.description: Round trip: UNICODE() extracts the code point of an accented character, UNICHAR() converts it straight back
UNICHAR_roundtrip_via_unicode.notes: UNICODE(char) then UNICHAR(that number) must reproduce the original character exactly

UNICHAR_astral_emoji.description: Code point beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane (U+1F600 GRINNING FACE emoji), requiring a UTF-16 surrogate pair internally
UNICHAR_astral_emoji.notes: 128512 decimal = U+1F600, the grinning-face emoji; modern Excel supports supplementary-plane code points via surrogate pairs

UNICHAR_zero_error.description: UNICHAR(0) is documented to raise #VALUE! (0 is not a valid character code point). Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/unichar-function-ffeb64f5-f131-44c6-b332-5cd72f0659b8 ("Number: ... Numbers <=0 ... UNICHAR returns the #VALUE! error value")

UNICHAR_negative_error.description: Negative code point is out of range -> #VALUE! per the same UNICHAR documentation as UNICHAR_zero_error

UNICODE_accented_char.description: Code point of an accented character beyond basic Latin (U+00E9)

UNICODE_astral_emoji.description: Code point of a supplementary-plane emoji character (U+1F600), the inverse of the UNICHAR_astral_emoji case

UNICODE_empty_string_error.description: Empty text has no first character to inspect -> #VALUE!. Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/unicode-function-adb74aaa-a2a5-4dde-aff6-966e4e81f16f (documented error handling: invalid/partial character data returns #VALUE!)

UNIQUE_basic.description: Basic unique list preserving first-occurrence order

UNIQUE_exactly_once.description: exactly_once=TRUE returns only items that appear exactly once

UNIQUE_by_column.description: by_col=TRUE compares whole columns instead of rows
UNIQUE_by_column.notes: Column A and column C are identical (1,1); unique columns are {1,2} and {1,1} but by_col dedups the repeated column, leaving 2 columns: [1,2] and [1,1] -> flatten to first row [1,2]

UNIQUE_no_duplicates.description: Input with no duplicates returns the input unchanged

UPPER_leaves_numbers_and_symbols.description: Digits and symbols have no case and are left unchanged

VALUE_numeric_string.description: Basic numeric-looking text string converts to a number

VALUE_percentage_string.description: A percentage-formatted text string converts to its underlying decimal, since Excel stores percentages internally as decimals (50% == 0.5)

VALUE_currency_string.description: Currency formatting (symbol + thousands separator) is stripped during conversion; matches Microsoft's own VALUE documentation example

VALUE_non_numeric_string_error.description: A string that isn't a recognized number/date/time format -> #VALUE!

VAR_basic.description: Sample variance (divides by n-1) of three evenly spaced values

VAR_from_range.description: Sample variance read from a cell range

VAR_two_values.description: Two values 5 either side of the mean give a sample variance of 50

VAR_ignores_text.description: Text and blank cells are ignored rather than counted

VAR.S_basic_two_points.description: Sample variance of two hand-verifiable values

VAR.S_wikipedia_dataset.description: Sample variance on the classic {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9} dataset; this is the square of STDEV.S_matches_STDEV_same_data's result (2.138089935299395^2)

VAR.S_single_value_div0.description: Sample variance needs n>=2 (divides by n-1); one value -> #DIV/0!

VARA_numbers_only.description: For pure numbers VARA equals VAR (sample variance dividing by n-1)

VARA_counts_text_as_zero.description: Unlike VAR, VARA counts text as 0, so {2,4,"x"} is treated as {2,4,0}: sample variance 4

VARP_textbook.description: Population variance (divides by n) of the classic 8-value example; equals STDEVP squared

VARP_from_range.description: Population variance read from a cell range

VARP_two_values.description: Population variance of two values divides the summed squared deviations by n

VLOOKUP_approximate_match.description: Approximate match requires ascending sorted first column
VLOOKUP_approximate_match.notes: 3 is between 2 and 4; approx match returns the row for the largest value <= lookup (2 -> 20)

VLOOKUP_col_index_out_of_range.description: col_index_num beyond the table width -> #REF! per Microsoft docs
VLOOKUP_col_index_out_of_range.notes: Microsoft docs specify #REF! for out-of-range col_index_num; record engines' ACTUAL error code here since this is a known point of cross-engine divergence

VLOOKUP_wildcard_exact_mode.description: Wildcards are honored even in exact-match mode
VLOOKUP_wildcard_exact_mode.notes: First row matching the a* wildcard pattern is 'apple'

VSTACK_two_rows.description: Vertically stack two 2-col rows into a 2x2 array

WEEKDAY_default_type1.description: Default return_type 1: Sunday=1..Saturday=7. Feb 14, 2008 is a Thursday. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/weekday-function-60e44483-2ed1-439f-8bd0-e404c190949a (worked example, WEEKDAY(A2)=5)

WEEKDAY_type2_monday_start.description: return_type 2: Monday=1..Sunday=7. Source: Microsoft WEEKDAY docs worked example, WEEKDAY(A2,2)=4.

WEEKDAY_type3_zero_based.description: return_type 3: Monday=0..Sunday=6 (zero-based). Thursday is 3 in this scheme.
WEEKDAY_type3_zero_based.notes: Per Microsoft's return_type table, mode 3 maps Monday..Sunday to 0..6; Thursday (the 4th weekday counting Monday=0) = 3.

WEEKDAY_type12_tuesday_start.description: return_type 12: Tuesday=1..Monday=7 (ISO-style variant start day). Thursday is the 3rd day in this scheme.
WEEKDAY_type12_tuesday_start.notes: Per Microsoft's return_type table, mode 12 maps Tuesday=1,Wed=2,Thu=3,...,Monday=7.

WEEKDAY_type16_saturday_start.description: return_type 16: Saturday=1..Friday=7. Thursday is the 6th day in this scheme.
WEEKDAY_type16_saturday_start.notes: Per Microsoft's return_type table, mode 16 maps Saturday=1,Sun=2,Mon=3,Tue=4,Wed=5,Thu=6,Fri=7.

WEEKDAY_invalid_return_type.description: An out-of-range return_type (not one of the documented 1,2,3,11-17 values) is a documented error condition.
WEEKDAY_invalid_return_type.notes: Microsoft docs: an invalid return_type raises #NUM!.

WEEKNUM_us_default_return_type_1.description: return_type 1 = US system, weeks start Sunday, week containing Jan 1 is always week 1. Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/weeknum-function-e5c43a03-b4ab-426c-b411-b18c13c75340

WEEKNUM_monday_start_return_type_2.description: return_type 2 = same 'week containing Jan 1 is week 1' system, but weeks start Monday
WEEKNUM_monday_start_return_type_2.notes: Jan 1, 2024 happens to BE a Monday, so it is both the week-1-by-Sunday-rule week AND the very first day of the week-1-by-Monday-rule week -- return_type 1 and 2 coincide at 1 for this specific date (see WEEKNUM_doc_example_* below for a date where they genuinely diverge)

WEEKNUM_doc_example_default.description: Microsoft's own documented example date/result for the default return_type (1)
WEEKNUM_doc_example_default.notes: Per Microsoft docs, WEEKNUM(3/9/2012) = 10 with default return_type

WEEKNUM_doc_example_monday_start_diverge.description: Same date as WEEKNUM_doc_example_default but return_type=2 (Monday-start): Microsoft's own docs show this returns a DIFFERENT week number (11, not 10) for the identical date -- the genuine return_type divergence
WEEKNUM_doc_example_monday_start_diverge.notes: Per Microsoft docs, WEEKNUM(3/9/2012,2) = 11, one more than the return_type=1 result of 10

WEEKNUM_return_type_21_is_iso_system.description: return_type 21 uses 'System 2': the week containing the year's first Thursday is week 1 (ISO 8601), a genuinely different algorithm from return_types 1/2/11-17 (all of which use 'week containing Jan 1 = week 1'). This should match ISOWEEKNUM(DATE(2023,1,1)) exactly -- see ISOWEEKNUM.json
WEEKNUM_return_type_21_is_iso_system.notes: Jan 1, 2023 is a Sunday; under the ISO rule it falls in the LAST ISO week (52) of 2022, not week 1 of 2023

WORKDAY_basic_no_holidays.description: 5 working days after Mon Jan 1, 2024, no holidays supplied
WORKDAY_basic_no_holidays.notes: Jan 1, 2024 (Mon) + 5 workdays, skipping the Jan 6-7 weekend, = Jan 8, 2024 = serial 45299

WORKDAY_with_single_holiday.description: Same start/offset as WORKDAY_basic_no_holidays but with Jan 3 excluded as a holiday, pushing the result one calendar day later
WORKDAY_with_single_holiday.notes: With Jan 3 excluded, the 5th workday becomes Jan 9, 2024 = serial 45300

WORKDAY_multiple_holidays_via_range.description: holidays argument as a multi-cell range (Jan 3 and Jan 4 both excluded)
WORKDAY_multiple_holidays_via_range.notes: With both Jan 3 and Jan 4 excluded, the 5th workday becomes Jan 10, 2024 = serial 45301

WORKDAY_negative_days_goes_backward.description: Negative days argument counts backward from start_date instead of forward. Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/workday-function-f764a5b7-05fc-4494-9486-60d494efbf33 ("A positive value for days yields a future date; a negative value yields a past date")
WORKDAY_negative_days_goes_backward.notes: Jan 10, 2024 (Wed) - 5 workdays, skipping the Jan 6-7 weekend, = Jan 3, 2024 = serial 45294

WORKDAY_INTL_next_workday.description: 1 working day after Fri Jul 24 = Mon Jul 27 (default Sat/Sun weekend)

WRAPCOLS_2.description: Wrap a 4-cell row into a grid 2 tall, filling by column

WRAPROWS_2.description: Wrap a 4-cell row into a 2-column grid, filling by row

XIRR_one_year_10pct.description: -1000 on 2026-01-01, +1100 exactly 365 days later: annualized return is exactly 10% (dates given as serials)

XLOOKUP_exact_match.description: Basic exact-match lookup returns the corresponding value

XLOOKUP_not_found_default_na.description: No if_not_found arg and no match -> #N/A

XLOOKUP_not_found_custom.description: Custom if_not_found value is returned when no match

XLOOKUP_match_mode_next_smaller.description: match_mode -1 (exact or next smaller item) with no exact match
XLOOKUP_match_mode_next_smaller.notes: 2.5 has no exact match; next-smaller is 2 -> 20

XLOOKUP_search_mode_last_to_first.description: search_mode -1 finds the LAST occurrence of a duplicated key
XLOOKUP_search_mode_last_to_first.notes: Two rows match 'x' (1 and 3); reverse search returns the later one

XLOOKUP_empty_lookup_array.description: Degenerate 1-cell lookup/return arrays where the cell is blank
XLOOKUP_empty_lookup_array.notes: A1 and B1 are blank; lookup value 'a' is not found

XNPV_zero_at_irr.description: Discounting the same two dated cashflows at their XIRR (10%) must give NPV = 0

XOR_odd_count_of_true.description: An ODD number of TRUE arguments (3) -> TRUE

XOR_even_count_of_true.description: An EVEN number of TRUE arguments (2) -> FALSE, matching docs' own example =XOR(3>0,2<9) -> FALSE

XOR_zero_true_is_even.description: Zero TRUE arguments counts as even -> FALSE, matching docs' own example =XOR(3>12,4>6) -> FALSE

XOR_single_true.description: A single TRUE argument (odd count = 1) -> TRUE

XOR_range_numeric_coercion.description: Numbers in a range are coerced to logical (0=FALSE, nonzero=TRUE); here two nonzero values -> 2 TRUEs (even) -> FALSE

YEAR_of_date.description: YEAR applied to a constructed date

YEAR_of_raw_serial_epoch.description: YEAR applied directly to the raw serial number 1 (the classic Excel epoch, serial 1 = Jan 1, 1900)
YEAR_of_raw_serial_epoch.notes: Serial 1 is Jan 1, 1900 in the 1900 date system; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 1900, got 1899

YEAR_ignores_time_fraction.description: A serial with a fractional (time-of-day) component still resolves to the correct calendar year
YEAR_ignores_time_fraction.notes: 45366 = 2024-03-15; the .75 fractional day (18:00) is ignored by YEAR

YEARFRAC_basis0_us_nasd_default.description: Default basis 0 (US/NASD 30/360): treats every month as 30 days. Days = 6*30+29 = 209, over a 360-day year -> 209/360. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/yearfrac-function-3844141e-c76d-4143-82b6-208454ddc6a8 (worked example rounds to 0.58055556)

YEARFRAC_basis1_actual_actual.description: basis 1 (Actual/actual): actual 211 calendar days between the two dates, divided by 366 since the enclosing 1-year span (Jan 2012-Jan 2013) is a leap year. Source: Microsoft YEARFRAC docs worked example rounds to 0.57650273.
YEARFRAC_basis1_actual_actual.notes: 211/366 = 0.5765027322404372, matching Microsoft's documented rounded example (0.57650273) to 8 decimal places. Actual/actual leap-year-boundary handling is a documented high-divergence area across spreadsheet engines.

YEARFRAC_basis2_actual_360.description: basis 2 (Actual/360): actual 211 calendar days divided by a fixed 360-day year. Source: Microsoft YEARFRAC docs basis table.

YEARFRAC_basis3_actual_365.description: basis 3 (Actual/365): actual 211 calendar days divided by a fixed 365-day year. Source: Microsoft YEARFRAC docs worked example rounds to 0.57808219.
YEARFRAC_basis3_actual_365.notes: 211/365 = 0.5780821917808219, matches Microsoft's documented rounded example exactly.

YEARFRAC_basis4_european_30_360.description: basis 4 (European 30/360). For this particular date pair neither day-of-month is the 31st, so the European day-count adjustment never triggers and the result equals basis 0's 209/360.
YEARFRAC_basis4_european_30_360.notes: European 30/360 only differs from US 30/360 when a start/end day-of-month is 31; with day 1 and day 30 as here, both conventions compute 209/360 identically.

YEARFRAC_invalid_basis_error.description: basis values outside 0-4 are documented as invalid.
YEARFRAC_invalid_basis_error.notes: Microsoft docs: 'invalid basis values (< 0 or > 4) return a #NUM! error.'

AVERAGEA_documented_text_counts_as_zero.description: Microsoft's documented example: four numbers plus a text cell, where the text is averaged in as 0
AVERAGEA_documented_text_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 5.6 and explains it as 'The cell with the text "Not available" is used in the calculation', i.e. (10+7+9+2+0)/5. The text cell contributes a 0 AND is counted in the divisor, which is exactly how AVERAGEA differs from AVERAGE (AVERAGE would give 28/4 = 7). This worked example is what resolves the same text-vs-ignored contradiction that appears on the MAXA, MINA and VARPA pages

AVERAGEA_logicals_true_one_false_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: TRUE is counted as 1 and FALSE as 0, both counted in the divisor
AVERAGEA_logicals_true_one_false_zero.notes: Excel documents TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0 for AVERAGEA: (1+1+0)/3 = 0.666666... -> 0.6667 at 4 dp. An engine using AVERAGE semantics (logicals in ranges ignored) would return 1

AVERAGEA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Empty cells are ignored entirely -- not counted as 0 and not counted in the divisor
AVERAGEA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Microsoft's second worked example on the same page averages a range plus a separate cell and still returns 5.6 because the empty cell is not counted. Empty cells are ignored by AVERAGEA (only text and logicals are coerced), so the answer here is (10+20)/2 = 15, not (10+0+20)/3

AVERAGEA_all_text_range.description: A range containing only text averages the coerced zeros rather than erroring
AVERAGEA_all_text_range.notes: Under the documented 'array or reference arguments that contain text evaluate as 0' rule both cells count as 0 and both count in the divisor: (0+0)/2 = 0. Microsoft's page also states explicitly that empty text ("") evaluates as 0

AVERAGEA_no_data_points_div0.description: A range of only empty cells has no data points at all
AVERAGEA_no_data_points_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's AVERAGEA page documents no error condition. But it does document that empty cells are ignored, so a range of only empty cells leaves no data points and the average's divisor is zero -- #DIV/0! is the only consistent result

DOLLARDE_documented_sixteenths.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 and 2/16 expressed in fractional notation converts to 1.125
DOLLARDE_documented_sixteenths.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.125. The fractional part .02 is read as 2 sixteenths: 1 + 2/16 = 1.125

DOLLARDE_documented_thirtyseconds.description: Documented example: 1.1 in thirty-seconds notation is 1 and 10/32
DOLLARDE_documented_thirtyseconds.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.3125. The fractional digits are padded to the width of the fraction denominator: .1 means 10 thirty-seconds, so 1 + 10/32 = 1.3125

DOLLARDE_non_integer_fraction_truncated.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a non-integer fraction is documented as truncated to an integer
DOLLARDE_non_integer_fraction_truncated.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is not an integer, it is truncated.' Truncating 16.9 to 16 reproduces the first documented example exactly, 1.125. An engine that rounded 16.9 to 17, or used it as-is, would return a different value

DOLLARDE_negative_dollar_value.description: A negative fractional dollar keeps its sign through the conversion
DOLLARDE_negative_dollar_value.notes: The magnitude converts the same way as the documented positive example and the sign is preserved: -(1 + 2/16) = -1.125

DOLLARDE_zero_fraction_div0.description: A fraction denominator of zero cannot be divided by
DOLLARDE_zero_fraction_div0.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is greater than or equal to 0 and less than 1, DOLLARDE returns the #DIV/0! error value.' Note the band is 0 <= fraction < 1, which is worded more widely than DOLLARFR's page (which names only fraction = 0) even though truncation makes the two equivalent in practice

DOLLARDE_negative_fraction_num_error.description: A negative fraction denominator is outside the documented domain
DOLLARDE_negative_fraction_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if fraction is less than 0

DOLLARFR_documented_sixteenths.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1.125 decimal converts to 1.02, read as 1 and 2/16
DOLLARFR_documented_sixteenths.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.02. 0.125 * 16 = 2 sixteenths, written in the fractional notation as .02

DOLLARFR_documented_thirtyseconds.description: Documented example: the same decimal in thirty-seconds is 1.04, read as 1 and 4/32
DOLLARFR_documented_thirtyseconds.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.04. 0.125 * 32 = 4 thirty-seconds, written as .04

DOLLARFR_round_trips_dollarde.description: DOLLARFR is documented as the inverse of DOLLARDE, so a round trip returns the original notation
DOLLARFR_round_trips_dollarde.notes: DOLLARDE(1.02,16) = 1.125 and DOLLARFR(1.125,16) = 1.02, so the composition is the identity on this value

DOLLARFR_non_integer_fraction_truncated.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a non-integer fraction is documented as truncated to an integer
DOLLARFR_non_integer_fraction_truncated.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is not an integer, it is truncated.' 16.9 truncates to 16, so the answer must match the first documented example, 1.02

DOLLARFR_zero_fraction_div0.description: A fraction denominator of zero is a division by zero
DOLLARFR_zero_fraction_div0.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is 0, DOLLARFR returns the #DIV/0! error value.' The DOLLARDE page words the same condition as the wider band 0 <= fraction < 1; because fraction is truncated first the two are equivalent, but the published wording differs between the pages

DOLLARFR_negative_fraction_num_error.description: A negative fraction denominator is outside the documented domain
DOLLARFR_negative_fraction_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if fraction is less than 0

FVSCHEDULE_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 unit of principal compounded at 9%, 11% then 10%
FVSCHEDULE_documented.notes: Microsoft publishes this example (=FVSCHEDULE(1,{0.09,0.11,0.1})) with the result displayed as 1.3309. The documented computation -- principal times the product of (1+rate) over the schedule -- is exact here: 1 * 1.09 * 1.11 * 1.10 = 1.330890 with no rounding, so 1.33089 is asserted at 7 dp rather than the page's 4-dp display

FVSCHEDULE_principal_scaled.description: The schedule is applied multiplicatively to any principal

FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: Excel documents empty cells in the schedule as zeros (a 0% period), not as skipped
FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'The values in schedule can be numbers or blank cells; any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE. Blank cells are taken as zeros (no interest).' So the blank is a 0% period: 1000 * 1.1 * 1.0 * 1.1 = 1210. An engine that silently skipped the blank would get the same answer here, but an engine that errored on the blank would not -- so this pins the documented 'blank means 0%' rule

FVSCHEDULE_negative_rate.description: A negative rate in the schedule shrinks the principal

FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.description: Non-numeric values in the schedule are an error, not a zero
FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE'. Note this is the opposite of most statistical functions, which ignore stray text in a reference, and it differs from an empty cell, which the same sentence documents as a zero rate

ISPMT_documented_first_month.description: Microsoft's documented example: interest paid in the first month of an 8,000,000 loan at 10% over three years
ISPMT_documented_first_month.notes: Microsoft's ISPMT page publishes no formula and no text example (its worked example is an image), and it contradicts itself on indexing: the argument table says per 'must be between 1 and Nper' while Remarks says 'ISPMT counts each period beginning with zero, not with one'. The even-principal formula ISPMT = pv * rate * (per/nper - 1) is confirmed by LibreOffice's own documented example (see the ISPMT_libreoffice_documented_example case) and reproduces Microsoft's own published figure of -64,814.8148 here: 8000000 * (0.1/12) * (1/36 - 1) = -64814.81481. Negative because it is cash paid out

ISPMT_documented_first_year.description: Documented example: interest paid in the first year of the same loan on an annual schedule
ISPMT_documented_first_year.notes: Same formula on an annual schedule: 8000000 * 0.1 * (1/3 - 1) = -533333.3333, matching the -533,333.33 figure published for this example

ISPMT_last_period_is_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: at per = nper the remaining balance is zero, so the interest is exactly zero
ISPMT_last_period_is_zero.notes: The documented formula pv*rate*(per/nper - 1) gives 8000000*0.1*(3/3 - 1) = 0. This is the clearest test of ISPMT's period indexing: an engine that treats per as 0-based, or that uses (1 - per/nper) with the opposite sign convention, will not return 0 here

ISPMT_period_zero_is_full_interest.description: At per = 0 the whole principal is still outstanding, so the interest is the full period charge
ISPMT_period_zero_is_full_interest.notes: 8000000 * 0.1 * (0/3 - 1) = -800000, i.e. one period's interest on the undiminished balance

ISPMT_libreoffice_documented_example.description: Cross-vendor check: LibreOffice's help page publishes a worked example for the same function
ISPMT_libreoffice_documented_example.notes: LibreOffice's Calc help documents ISPMT(Rate; Period; TotalPeriods; Invest) with the worked example =ISPMT(1%;18;24;120000) = -300. That is exactly pv * rate * (per/nper - 1) = 120000 * 0.01 * (18/24 - 1) = -300, so both vendors' documentation agrees on the formula and on the sign convention

ISPMT_zero_nper_div0.description: A zero number of periods divides by zero inside the per/nper term
ISPMT_zero_nper_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's ISPMT page documents no error conditions at all. The formula confirmed by both vendors' worked examples divides per by nper, so nper = 0 is a division by zero and #DIV/0! is the consistent result

KURT_documented_sample.description: Microsoft's documented example: kurtosis of the ten-value sample 3,4,5,2,3,4,5,6,4,7
KURT_documented_sample.notes: Excel documents this example's result as -0.1518. Independently derived from the documented excess-kurtosis formula n(n+1)/((n-1)(n-2)(n-3)) * SUM(((x-mean)/s)^4) - 3(n-1)^2/((n-2)(n-3)) with n = 10, mean 4.3, s = 1.4181 -> -0.15179964

KURT_leptokurtic_outlier_positive.description: A heavy single outlier raises kurtosis above zero
KURT_leptokurtic_outlier_positive.notes: Derived from the documented formula: mean 2.6, s = 3.5777; standardized deviations are four copies of -0.44721 and one of 1.78885; sum of 4th powers = 10.4; n(n+1)/((n-1)(n-2)(n-3)) = 30/24 = 1.25; 1.25*10.4 = 13; minus 3(n-1)^2/((n-2)(n-3)) = 48/6 = 8; 13-8 = 5

KURT_fewer_than_four_points_div0.description: The (n-3) factor is undefined below four data points
KURT_fewer_than_four_points_div0.notes: Excel documents #DIV/0! if there are fewer than four data points, because (n-3) is zero

KURT_zero_variance_div0.description: Identical values give a zero sample standard deviation
KURT_zero_variance_div0.notes: Excel documents #DIV/0! if the sample standard deviation of the data is zero

LENB_ascii_string.description: Microsoft's documented example string: byte length of an 11-character ASCII string
LENB_ascii_string.notes: Microsoft's LEN/LENB page uses 'Phoenix, AZ' as its worked example and publishes LEN = 11. The DBCS rule (see the LENB_non_ascii_characters case) cannot change the answer here because every character is single-byte under either reading. NOTE: the current live page now states 'The LENB function is deprecated' and has dropped the DBCS explanation entirely

LENB_empty_string.description: An empty string has zero bytes
LENB_empty_string.notes: No characters means no bytes, under either the DBCS or the non-DBCS rule

LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.description: Spaces are characters and are counted, including leading and trailing ones
LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.notes: Microsoft documents 'Spaces count as characters' for the text argument of LEN/LENB; the string here is two spaces, three letters and three spaces = 8

LENB_number_argument_coerced.description: A numeric argument is converted to its text representation before measuring
LENB_number_argument_coerced.notes: The number 1234 becomes the four-character string "1234", so the byte length is 4 in a non-DBCS default language

LENB_non_ascii_characters.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: two CJK characters, where the byte count depends on the DBCS language rule
LENB_non_ascii_characters.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's archived LEN/LENB page: 'LENB counts 2 bytes per character only when a DBCS language is set as the default language. Otherwise LENB behaves the same as LEN, counting 1 byte per character', with DBCS listed as Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional) and Korean. The harness runs under a non-DBCS default locale, so the documented answer is 2 (LEN semantics). An engine that always counts raw UTF-8 or UTF-16 bytes returns 6 or 4 instead -- recording which one each engine does is the point of this case; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 2, got 4

LENB_propagates_error.description: An error argument propagates instead of being measured
LENB_propagates_error.notes: The argument evaluates to #DIV/0! before LENB sees it, so the error is the result

MAXA_documented_logical_beats_numbers.description: Microsoft's documented example: the largest value in a range where TRUE is counted as 1
MAXA_documented_logical_beats_numbers.notes: Excel documents MAXA as evaluating a logical TRUE in a range as 1, so the answer is 1 rather than 0.5; MAX over the same range would return 0.5 because MAX ignores logicals in ranges

MAXA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: all-negative numbers plus a text cell -- Excel counts the text as 0, which becomes the maximum
MAXA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft's MAXA page carries two remarks that contradict each other for this exact input: 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)' and, one line later, 'Empty cells and text values in the array or reference are ignored'. We assert the text-evaluates-as-0 reading, because AVERAGEA's page carries the identical contradictory pair and settles it with a worked example (28/5 = 5.6) in which range text counts as 0. Under that reading the answer is 0 (0 > -3); under the 'ignored' reading it would be -3. The point of this case is to record which reading each engine actually implements

MAXA_false_in_range_counts_as_zero.description: FALSE in a range is evaluated as 0, so it wins over negative numbers
MAXA_false_in_range_counts_as_zero.notes: Excel documents logical FALSE as 0 for MAXA; 0 > -1 so the maximum is 0

MAXA_direct_logical_argument.description: A logical typed directly as an argument is also coerced (TRUE -> 1)
MAXA_direct_logical_argument.notes: Excel documents that MAXA evaluates TRUE as 1 whether it comes from a range or is typed as an argument

MAXA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Truly empty cells are ignored (they are not counted as 0)
MAXA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Excel documents empty cells in a reference as ignored by MAXA (this remark is not contradicted elsewhere on the page, unlike the text remark), so the maximum is the largest actual number, -2, and NOT 0

MAXA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.description: A non-numeric string typed directly as an argument is documented as evaluating to 0, which then wins
MAXA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's MAXA page: 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)'. Under that rule the literal "abc" becomes 0, which is larger than -5. (MAX's page carries the opposite rule -- text that cannot be translated into numbers causes an error -- so this case checks that an engine applies the A-variant rule and not MAX's); MISMATCH vs expected: expected 0, got '#VALUE!'

MAXA_error_value_propagates.description: An error value passed as an argument propagates instead of being coerced
MAXA_error_value_propagates.notes: Error values are not among the things MAXA coerces; NA() produces #N/A and that error is the result of the whole expression

MINA_documented_false_is_smallest.description: Microsoft's documented example: FALSE in the range evaluates to 0, which is the smallest value
MINA_documented_false_is_smallest.notes: Microsoft's worked example for this exact data returns 0, explained on the page as 'Because a value of FALSE evaluates to 0, it is the smallest'. MIN over the same range would return 0.2, because MIN ignores logicals in a reference

MINA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: all-positive numbers plus a text cell -- Excel counts the text as 0, which becomes the minimum
MINA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft's MINA page carries the same self-contradicting pair as MAXA ('text ... evaluate as 0' vs 'text values in the array or reference are ignored'). We assert the text-evaluates-as-0 reading, which AVERAGEA's worked example confirms for the identical wording. Under that reading the answer is 0 (0 < 3); under the 'ignored' reading it would be 3. This case records which reading the engine implements

MINA_true_only_range.description: A range of logical TRUEs is a range of 1s
MINA_true_only_range.notes: Both cells evaluate to 1, so the minimum is 1

MINA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Truly empty cells are ignored rather than counted as 0
MINA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Excel documents empty cells as ignored by MINA; if blanks counted as 0 the answer would be 0, so this distinguishes blank handling from text handling

MINA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.description: A non-numeric string typed directly as an argument is documented as evaluating to 0, which then wins
MINA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's MINA page: 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)'. Under that rule the literal "abc" becomes 0, which is smaller than 5. MIN's page carries the opposite rule, so this case checks the A-variant rule is applied; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 0, got '#VALUE!'

MINA_error_value_propagates.description: An error value passed as an argument propagates instead of being coerced
MINA_error_value_propagates.notes: Error values are not coerced by MINA; NA() produces #N/A and that error is the result

MIRR_documented_five_years.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 5 years of cash flows, 10% finance rate, 12% reinvestment rate
MIRR_documented_five_years.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 12.61% (the live page displays it rounded to 13%). Independently derived from the documented formula MIRR = (-NPV(reinvest, positives)*(1+reinvest)^n / (NPV(finance, negatives)*(1+finance)))^(1/(n-1)) - 1 with n = 6 values: the reinvested inflows are carried forward at 12% and the single -120000 outflow discounted at 10%; the 5th root of the ratio gives 0.12609413 -> 0.1261 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_first_three_years.description: Same doc example truncated to the first three years of inflows, which is still a net loss
MIRR_documented_first_three_years.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as -4.80% (displayed rounded to -5%). Same formula with n = 4 values (-120000, 39000, 30000, 21000): the reinvested inflows do not recover the outflow, so the cube root of the ratio is below 1 -> -0.04804466 -> -0.048 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.description: Same cash flows with the reinvestment rate raised from 12% to 14%
MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 13.48% (displayed rounded to 13%). Raising only the reinvestment rate raises the future value of the positive flows; recomputing the documented formula gives 0.13475911 -> 0.1348 at 4 dp

MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.description: A zero cash flow is neither an inflow nor an outflow, so it only contributes to the period count
MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.notes: Excel documents that MIRR ignores text, logical values and empty cells in a reference but INCLUDES cells with the value zero. Zero belongs to neither the positive nor the negative NPV; with finance = reinvest = 0.1, the future value of the inflows is 600*1.1 + 700 = 1360 and the compounded present value of the outflow is -1000, with n = 4 values, so (1360/1000)^(1/3) - 1 = 0.10793165 -> 0.1079

MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.description: Excel documents #DIV/0! when values contains no negative (or no positive) number
MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.notes: With no negative cash flow the denominator NPV of the outflows is zero, and Excel documents that MIRR requires at least one positive and one negative value or it returns #DIV/0!

NORM.DIST_cumulative_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: cumulative distribution at x=42 for mean 40, sd 1.5
NORM.DIST_cumulative_documented.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 0.9087888. Independently verified against the normal CDF: z = (42-40)/1.5 = 1.33333, Phi(1.33333) = 0.90878878 -> 0.9087888 at 7 dp

NORM.DIST_pdf_documented.description: Same parameters with cumulative FALSE returns the probability density instead
NORM.DIST_pdf_documented.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 0.10934. Independently verified from the density formula exp(-(x-mean)^2/(2*sd^2))/(sd*sqrt(2*pi)) = 0.10934005 -> 0.10934 at 5 dp

NORM.DIST_standard_at_mean.description: At the mean the cumulative normal is exactly one half
NORM.DIST_standard_at_mean.notes: The normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so the CDF at x = mean is 0.5 for any positive standard deviation

NORM.DIST_zero_stdev_num_error.description: A standard deviation of zero is outside the domain
NORM.DIST_zero_stdev_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! when standard_dev is less than or equal to 0

NORM.DIST_text_argument_error.description: A non-numeric argument is a value error rather than a numeric-domain error
NORM.DIST_text_argument_error.notes: Excel documents #VALUE! when x, mean or standard_dev is non-numeric

NORM.INV_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: the inverse of the cumulative normal, which round-trips NORM.DIST
NORM.INV_documented.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 42.000002. The probability 0.908789 is the rounded NORM.DIST(42,40,1.5,TRUE) value, so the inverse returns 42.00000201; rounding to 4 dp gives 42

NORM.INV_standard_median.description: The median of a standard normal is zero
NORM.INV_standard_median.notes: Phi(0) = 0.5, so the inverse of 0.5 with mean 0 is exactly the mean, 0

NORM.INV_shifts_with_mean.description: The 50th percentile of any normal distribution is its mean
NORM.INV_shifts_with_mean.notes: Symmetry puts the median at the mean regardless of the standard deviation

NORM.INV_probability_zero_num_error.description: Probability 0 lies on the open-interval boundary of the domain
NORM.INV_probability_zero_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if probability <= 0 or probability >= 1 (the normal quantile is unbounded at the endpoints)

NORM.INV_negative_stdev_num_error.description: A negative standard deviation is outside the domain

NORM.S.DIST_cumulative_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: standard normal cumulative distribution at z = 1.333333
NORM.S.DIST_cumulative_documented.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 0.908788726. Independently verified against the standard normal CDF: Phi(1.333333) = 0.908788726 -> 0.908789 at 6 dp

NORM.S.DIST_density_documented.description: Same z with cumulative FALSE returns the standard normal density
NORM.S.DIST_density_documented.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 0.164010148. Independently verified from the standard normal density exp(-z^2/2)/sqrt(2*pi) = 0.164010148 -> 0.164010 at 6 dp

NORM.S.DIST_zero_cumulative.description: The standard normal CDF at zero is one half
NORM.S.DIST_zero_cumulative.notes: The standard normal is symmetric about 0, so Phi(0) = 0.5 exactly

NORM.S.DIST_symmetry_negative_z.description: Symmetry check: Phi(-z) + Phi(z) must be exactly 1
NORM.S.DIST_symmetry_negative_z.notes: Phi(-z) = 1 - Phi(z) for the standard normal, so the two cumulative values sum to 1 for any z

NORM.S.DIST_text_argument_error.description: A non-numeric z is a value error
NORM.S.DIST_text_argument_error.notes: 'If z is nonnumeric, NORM.S.DIST returns the #VALUE! error' -- the only error condition documented for this function

NORM.S.INV_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: the inverse standard normal at probability 0.908789
NORM.S.INV_documented.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.3333347. The independently computed quantile is 1.33333467, which rounds to 1.333335 at 6 dp (the input probability is itself a 6-dp rounding of Phi(1.333333), which is why the answer is not exactly 1.333333)

NORM.S.INV_median.description: The 50th percentile of the standard normal is zero
NORM.S.INV_median.notes: Phi(0) = 0.5, so the inverse of 0.5 is exactly 0

NORM.S.INV_round_trip.description: NORM.S.INV inverts NORM.S.DIST exactly, so a full round trip returns the original z
NORM.S.INV_round_trip.notes: The two functions are documented as inverses of each other; feeding the unrounded CDF value straight back must recover z = 1.5 to well within 6 dp

NORM.S.INV_probability_one_num_error.description: Probability 1 is outside the open domain (the quantile is unbounded there)
NORM.S.INV_probability_one_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if probability <= 0 or probability >= 1

NORM.S.INV_negative_probability_num_erro.description: A negative probability is outside the domain
NORM.S.INV_negative_probability_num_erro.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if probability <= 0 or probability >= 1

PDURATION_documented_annual.description: Microsoft's documented example: periods required for 2,000 to reach 2,200 at 2.5% per period
PDURATION_documented_annual.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 3.86 periods. Derived from the documented formula (LN(fv) - LN(pv)) / LN(1 + rate) = LN(1.1)/LN(1.025) = 3.85986616

PDURATION_documented_monthly.description: Documented example: months for 1,000 to reach 1,200 at 2.5% annual interest
PDURATION_documented_monthly.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 87.6 months. Same formula with a monthly rate of 0.025/12 -> LN(1.2)/LN(1+0.0020833) = 87.60547642

PDURATION_doubling_at_100pct.description: A clean closed-form case: doubling at a 100% rate takes exactly one period

PDURATION_zero_rate_num_error.description: A rate of zero makes LN(1+rate) zero, so the value never grows
PDURATION_zero_rate_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if rate is less than or equal to 0 (with no growth the target is never reached)

PDURATION_negative_fv_num_error.description: A non-positive future value is outside the logarithm's domain
PDURATION_negative_fv_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if pv or fv is less than or equal to 0, since the formula takes their natural logarithms

RRI_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: the equivalent interest rate for 10,000 growing to 11,000 over 96 months
RRI_documented.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 0.0009933 (0.09933% per month). Derived from the documented formula RRI = (fv/pv)^(1/nper) - 1 = 1.1^(1/96) - 1 = 0.00099331

RRI_quadrupling_over_two_periods.description: A clean closed-form case: quadrupling in two periods is exactly 100% per period
RRI_quadrupling_over_two_periods.notes: (400/100)^(1/2) - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 exactly, i.e. a 100% return each period

RRI_loss_gives_negative_rate.description: A future value below the present value gives a negative equivalent rate

RRI_zero_nper_num_error.description: Zero periods makes the exponent 1/nper undefined
RRI_zero_nper_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if nper is less than or equal to 0 (and if pv is less than or equal to 0); MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#DIV/0!'

RRI_zero_pv_num_error.description: A present value of zero makes the fv/pv ratio undefined
RRI_zero_pv_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if pv is less than or equal to 0

SKEW_documented_sample.description: Microsoft's documented example: skewness of the ten-value sample 3,4,5,2,3,4,5,6,4,7
SKEW_documented_sample.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 0.359543. Independently derived from the documented formula n/((n-1)(n-2)) * SUM(((x-mean)/s)^3) with n = 10, mean 4.3 and sample standard deviation s = 1.4181 -> 0.35954307

SKEW_symmetric_data_is_zero.description: A perfectly symmetric sample has zero skewness
SKEW_symmetric_data_is_zero.notes: The cubed standardized deviations of a symmetric set cancel exactly in pairs, so the sum and therefore the skewness is 0

SKEW_right_tail_is_positive.description: A single large outlier pulls the skewness positive
SKEW_right_tail_is_positive.notes: Derived from the documented formula: mean 3, s = 4, standardized deviations -0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 1.5; sum of cubes = 3.0; n/((n-1)(n-2)) = 4/6 = 0.66667; 0.66667*3 = 2 exactly

SKEW_fewer_than_three_points_div0.description: The n/((n-1)(n-2)) factor is undefined below three data points
SKEW_fewer_than_three_points_div0.notes: Excel documents #DIV/0! if there are fewer than three data points, because (n-2) is zero

SKEW_zero_variance_div0.description: Identical values give a zero sample standard deviation, which cannot be divided by
SKEW_zero_variance_div0.notes: Excel documents #DIV/0! if the sample standard deviation is zero, since the formula standardizes each deviation by s

T_documented_text_passthrough.description: Microsoft's documented example: T returns text arguments unchanged
T_documented_text_passthrough.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If value is or refers to text, T returns value.' The page's own example returns Rainfall for a cell holding that text

T_documented_number_gives_empty_text.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a number is not text, so T returns empty text rather than the number
T_documented_number_gives_empty_text.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If value does not refer to text, T returns "" (empty text)', and the page's example for the value 19 says 'Because the second value is a number, empty text is returned'. An engine that coerced the number to a string would return "19" instead

T_documented_logical_gives_empty_text.description: A logical value is also not text, so the result is empty text
T_documented_logical_gives_empty_text.notes: Microsoft's example table covers this case explicitly: 'Because the third value is a logical value, empty text is returned'. There is no TRUE -> "TRUE" coercion

T_text_cell_reference.description: A reference to a cell holding text returns that text
T_text_cell_reference.notes: The referenced value is text, so T passes it through unchanged

T_numeric_cell_reference_gives_empty_tex.description: A reference to a cell holding a number returns empty text
T_numeric_cell_reference_gives_empty_tex.notes: The referenced value is a number, which is not text, so T returns ""

T_propagates_error.description: An error value passed to T propagates rather than becoming empty text
T_propagates_error.notes: Error values propagate through T; the argument itself evaluates to #DIV/0! and that error is the result of the whole expression

VAR.P_documented_population_variance.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten tool readings
VAR.P_documented_population_variance.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 678.84, alongside VAR.S over the same data as 754.27. Independently derived: mean 1328.6, sum of squared deviations 6788.4, divided by n = 10 = 678.84 (VAR.S divides by n-1 and so gives 754.2667)

VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: the paired case to VARPA -- VAR.P IGNORES text rather than counting it as 0
VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.notes: Microsoft's VAR.P page is unambiguous where VARPA's is not: 'Empty cells, logical values, text, or error values in the array or reference are ignored.' Data are 1, 2, 3 with mean 2; squared deviations 1+0+1 = 2, divided by n = 3 gives 0.66667 -> 0.6667. The identical range under VARPA gives 1.25, so the two cases together pin down the coercion rule

VAR.P_ignores_logicals_in_range.description: A logical inside a referenced range is ignored, so only the numbers are used
VAR.P_ignores_logicals_in_range.notes: Microsoft documents logical values in a reference as ignored by VAR.P. Data 4 and 8, mean 6, squared deviations 4+4 = 8, divided by n = 2 gives 4

VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.description: One data point has zero population variance
VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.notes: Population variance divides by n, so a single point gives 0/1 = 0

VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.description: A range holding only text leaves VAR.P with no data points
VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: the VAR.P page documents no error condition. Text in a reference is documented as ignored, so n = 0 and the population denominator is zero -- #DIV/0!

VARPA_documented_population_variance.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten numeric readings
VARPA_documented_population_variance.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 678.84 (the same page shows VAR over the same data as 754.27). Independently derived: mean = 13286/10 = 1328.6, sum of squared deviations = 6788.4, divided by n = 10 (population denominator) = 678.84

VARPA_text_counted_as_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a text cell is counted as the value 0 and included in n
VARPA_text_counted_as_zero.notes: Microsoft's VARPA page states 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)' (and, contradictorily, that range text is ignored -- resolved the same way as AVERAGEA's worked example resolves it). Under the counts-as-0 reading data become 1, 2, 3, 0 with mean 1.5; squared deviations 0.25+0.25+2.25+2.25 = 5, divided by n = 4 gives 1.25. An engine using VAR.P semantics on this range would return 0.6667 instead

VARPA_logicals_true_is_one.description: TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0 inside a range
VARPA_logicals_true_is_one.notes: Microsoft documents 'Arguments that contain TRUE evaluate as 1; arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0' for VARPA: data 1, 0, 0 with mean 1/3; squared deviations (2/3)^2 + (1/3)^2 + (1/3)^2 = 2/3, divided by n = 3 gives 0.22222... -> 0.2222

VARPA_single_value_is_zero.description: Population variance of a single data point is defined (0), unlike sample variance
VARPA_single_value_is_zero.notes: The population denominator is n, not n-1, so one data point gives 0/1 = 0 rather than a division-by-zero error

VARPA_empty_range_div0.description: With no data points at all there is nothing to divide by
VARPA_empty_range_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's VARPA page documents NO error condition at all. Empty cells are documented as ignored, so an all-empty range leaves n = 0 and the population denominator is zero; #DIV/0! is the consistent result

VDB_documented_first_year.description: Microsoft's documented example: first year's depreciation of a $2,400 asset with a 10-year life
VDB_documented_first_year.notes: Excel documents this example's result as $480.00. Derived from the default double-declining factor of 2: 2400 * 2/10 = 480 for the first full period, which still exceeds the straight-line alternative so no switch occurs

VDB_documented_months_6_to_18.description: Documented example: depreciation between the 6th and 18th month of a 120-month life
VDB_documented_months_6_to_18.notes: Excel documents this example's result as $396.31. Independently derived by accumulating the double-declining amount month by month (rate 2/120), summing months 6 through 17 -> 396.30605

VDB_documented_factor_1_5.description: Documented example: the same span with an explicit 1.5 declining-balance factor
VDB_documented_factor_1_5.notes: Excel documents this example's result as $311.81. Same month-by-month accumulation with rate 1.5/120 -> 311.80894

VDB_documented_partial_period.description: Documented example: a fractional end_period, where the period's depreciation is prorated
VDB_documented_partial_period.notes: Excel documents this example's result as $315.00. The first period's depreciation at factor 1.5 is 2400*1.5/10 = 360, and 0.875 of that period is 360*0.875 = 315 exactly

VDB_no_switch_true_keeps_declining_balan.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: no_switch TRUE suppresses the straight-line crossover in the late periods
VDB_no_switch_true_keeps_declining_balan.notes: Derived from the documented algorithm. Book values after three double-declining periods (rate 0.4) are 1000 -> 600 -> 360 -> 216. With no_switch TRUE periods 4 and 5 stay on declining balance: 216*0.4 = 86.4 and 129.6*0.4 = 51.84, totalling 138.24. With the default no_switch FALSE the same call switches to straight line and totals 216.00, so this case pins down whether the flag is honoured

VDB_negative_life_num_error.description: A negative life is outside the documented domain
VDB_negative_life_num_error.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's VDB page states 'All arguments except no_switch must be positive numbers' but does not name the error code. #NUM! is Excel's documented error for an out-of-domain argument across the rest of the depreciation family (DB, DDB, SLN, SYD all document #NUM! for a negative life), so #NUM! is what is asserted here
